headline: High: shared filesystem, MCP, and broad egress create prompt-injection, leakage, and action-conflict risks between open-webui and Windsurf.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: open-webui can ingest MCP/OpenAPI tool outputs and browser/file content, while Windsurf can read clipboard/workspace files and use MCP. That creates a plausible default bridge where attacker-controlled content from one can be treated as instructions by the other. The shared channel is stronger than manual copy-paste, so uncertainty should not lower severity.
conditions: IF open-webui forwards tool or browser output into a shared workspace or clipboard that Windsurf reads, injection is possible.
IF Windsurf auto-applies instructions from workspace files or clipboard content, attacker-controlled text can steer actions.
mitigations: Disable clipboard-based handoff between the apps.
Keep the agents on separate workspaces or containers.
Turn off auto-execute in Windsurf.
Restrict open-webui to trusted MCP servers only.
requires-engineering: add provenance tags before any cross-agent content transfer.

B_data_leakage.rationale: open-webui touches prompts, chat messages, documents, files, notes, calendar events, persistent memory, and API keys, and it can call external APIs. Windsurf reads and writes workspace files with broad network egress. If they share a workspace or file path, sensitive content can flow from open-webui into Windsurf and then out through model or tool calls, making leakage plausible in default use.
conditions: IF both agents access the same mounted directory or workspace, files and secrets can be exposed across the pair.
IF Windsurf sends workspace contents to its model proxy or MCP servers, data from open-webui can leave the local boundary.
mitigations: Separate the agents onto different directories.
Remove secrets from any shared workspace.
Disable broad network egress where possible.
Use a dedicated redaction step before copying artifacts.
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent ACLs on shared storage.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Both agents have overlapping write and network capabilities: open-webui can use plugins/MCP/OpenAPI and broad egress, while Windsurf can execute shell, modify git state, write files, and use MCP. With Windsurf's shared state via local filesystem and open-webui's persistent shared sessions, concurrent edits can race and corrupt files or git history. No locking mechanism is documented here, so uncertainty pushes upward.
conditions: IF both agents modify the same repository or directory, file and git conflicts can occur.
IF open-webui and Windsurf issue concurrent writes without external locking, state corruption is possible.
mitigations: Assign each agent a separate working tree.
Pause one agent before the other writes.
Avoid concurrent git operations.
Use file-level locks for shared paths.
requires-engineering: add orchestrator-level coordination and locking.

D_cascading_error.rationale: open-webui can generate content from browsers, search, and tool servers, and Windsurf can act on workspace files and terminal commands. If Windsurf treats open-webui output as authoritative, a mistaken or malicious answer can cascade into code changes, package installs, or shell execution. The pair therefore supports an unsafe generate-then-act chain in default workflows.
conditions: IF Windsurf uses open-webui output as a source of truth without verification, downstream actions can be wrong.
IF open-webui supplies code, facts, or citations that Windsurf commits or executes, errors cascade.
mitigations: Require human review before shell or git actions.
Cross-check open-webui outputs against primary sources.
Disable auto-execute in Windsurf.
Keep generated artifacts separate from executable code.
requires-engineering: add verification gates before action tools.

E_compliance.rationale: open-webui handles API keys, persistent memory, documents, and calendar events, while Windsurf handles source code and open files with local filesystem sharing. The pair can therefore mix sensitive and regulated data in one workspace, creating retention and residency ambiguity. The profiles do not prove a specific jurisdiction mismatch, so medium is the highest supportable level.
conditions: IF regulated data is placed in a shared workspace, retention and access controls may diverge.
IF one agent logs or persists content longer than the other, compliance obligations can be violated.
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of shared workspaces.
Review logging and retention settings in both tools.
Use separate accounts or tenants where possible.
Delete temporary artifacts after each task.
requires-engineering: document residency and retention boundaries per agent.
